newsitem.title: UK: Markets prefer EMU delay to soft euro - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Markets prefer EMU delay to soft euro - analysts.

text.p: A delay could deal a body blow to a single European currency, but may prove less disastrous for financial markets than an attempt to go ahead without strict adherence to the Maastricht criteria, economists said on Monday.
Worries that European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will be delayed from its proposed start on January 1, 1999 have resurged recently -- sending tremors through the markets.
"At the moment, the market is just about betting that the timetable will be adhered to, and sees that as the most important issue," said Stephen King, chief economist at HSBC-James Capel in London.
"But as the year goes on, and it starts to look like Germany will not meet the criteria, there will be mounting pressure for a delay," he said.
A delay in order to ensure the new euro currency will have a strong start, could also mean investors bail out of peripheral European markets, in favour of safe havens such as Germany and Britain.
That haemorrhage of investment could cut chances of the project going ahead, as Italian and Spanish bonds see spreads over German Bunds widening as convergence trades are undone.

Doubts gained strength on Saturday, when Herbert Hax, head of the "five wise men" economic advisory panel said Germany would in all likelihood miss the Maastricht Treaty's budget deficit and government debt goals this year.
The Treaty limits the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, while gross government debt must not be more than 60 percent of GDP in 1997.

Analysts said the central problem is that if Germany fails to come up to the required standards to join a single currency, there will be a tendency to relax those standards. That would in turn mean countries such as Italy could argue that any relaxation must apply to them as well.

"Germany is currently relying on strict adherence to keep Italy and Spain out," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at the London Bond Broking Company here. "If it can't use that, then without a delay, we are facing no euro or a soft euro."

A soft euro -- where the currency is weaker than the mark, the current European core currency -- would be the worst of all worlds, said Lewis, having ramifications which could include unstable exchange rate and a trade war with the United States.
"If the euro is soft, the U.S would be less competitive, and could retaliate," said Lewis.

Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe said the euro's strength in the first five years depends on its starting with the Maastricht criteria -- the macroeconomic principles which unperpin a strong currency -- intact.
He said Italy and Spain are less concerned than the hardcore European countries about the prospect of a soft euro.

"The high yielders are happy, because a soft euro would still be better than the peseta, for example," he said. "High yielders are also the most sensitive to a delay, as there's a feeling they have made a once-and-for-all effort that they may not be able to repeat."
Talk of a delay also becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Currency turbulence before and after such an annoucement could effectively derail the project, analysts said.
"If there's a feeling that EMU will not be on time, it will mean a weaker lira which will in turn feed into higher inflation," said Lewis.
The solution, according to some economists is a very tightly managed delay, with strict deadlines and tough assessment. But opinion varied about how long a delay the market could brook.
Fishwick said a "long and tortuous delay" would lead to speculation the criteria would be eased, while King said a short delay would not allow countries to put their books in order.
"(German Chancellor) Kohl has the opportunity at the moment to delay EMU, and present it as a favour to the peripherals," said Lewis. "That may prove the best thing he can do for everyone."
